name: Lobules I–IV
summary: Lobules I to IV form the anterior part of the anterior lobe of the cerebellum, the lingula, central lobule and culmen of the vermis with their small hemispheric wings, tucked under the tentorium in front of the primary fissure and behind the superior medullary velum. They are spinocerebellar cortex receiving the spinocerebellar tracts from the legs and trunk and projecting through the fastigial and interposed nuclei to the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal systems, so they regulate muscle tone, posture and the gait of the lower limbs. Their degeneration in chronic alcoholism produces the classic anterior lobe syndrome of a wide-based ataxic gait with relatively preserved arm coordination, and they are compressed by superior vermian and tentorial masses.

anatomy.location: Anterior lobe of the cerebellum from the superior medullary velum back to the primary fissure, rostral and superior to lobule V, mostly vermian with small hemispheric extensions, lying beneath the tentorium and behind the midbrain and the superior cerebellar peduncles.

afferents.via: dorsal and ventral spinocerebellar tracts via the inferior and superior peduncles
climbing fibers via the inferior peduncle

function: The anterior lobe cortex receives the dorsal and ventral spinocerebellar tracts (leg and trunk proprioception and copies of spinal interneuron activity) and the cuneocerebellar tract from the arm, together with pontine input from the sensorimotor cortex and olivary climbing fibers; its Purkinje cells inhibit the fastigial and interposed nuclei, which drive the vestibulospinal, reticulospinal and rubrospinal systems and the ventrolateral thalamus. The result is continuous adjustment of limb tone and of the timing of the leg muscles in walking and standing, with a somatotopic map in which the legs are represented anteriorly. Loss produces gait and stance ataxia and hypotonia of the legs.

bestView.label: anterior lobe of the vermis in front of the primary fissure

imaging.normalAppearance: The anterosuperior vermis on midline sagittal images between the fourth ventricle roof and the primary fissure, folded into narrow folia; atrophy widens its fissures before the rest of the cerebellum.

pathology.finding: Selective atrophy of the anterior superior vermis with widened folia on sagittal images, in a patient with gait ataxia and relatively spared limbs.
Restricted diffusion of the superior cerebellum including the anterior lobe with gait and limb ataxia and, when swollen, brainstem compression.

pathology.pathology: Superior vermian compression by a tentorial meningioma
pathology.finding: Enhancing tentorial mass indenting the anterior lobe with progressive gait ataxia.

lesionEffects.deficit: Wide-based, unsteady gait and truncal instability
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of spinocerebellar regulation of leg and trunk muscles
Loss of anterior lobe facilitation of tone through the fastigial and vestibulospinal system
The arm representation lies in more posterior lobules

examination: Tandem gait and Romberg with eyes open (cerebellar patients sway with eyes open)
Heel-shin test compared with finger-nose test
pearls: Anterior lobe atrophy is the cerebellar signature of alcohol: the legs go before the arms
The anterior vermis on a sagittal MRI is the first place to look for cerebellar atrophy
Gait ataxia with normal finger-nose testing is anterior lobe, not hemisphere

citations.section: Somatomotor Topography of the Cerebellum Is Evident within the Individual
